fuel.e: From Middle English fuayle, from Old French fouaille, feuaille (“firewood, kindling”), from feu (“fire”), from Late Latin focus (“fire”), from Latin focus (“hearth”), whence English focus.
fuel.g: Substance consumed to provide energy through combustion, or through chemical or nuclear reaction.

fugitive.e: From Middle English fugitive, fugityve, fugityf, fugitife, fugytif, fugitif, from Latin fugitīvus, from fugitō, from fugiō.
fugitive.g: A person who flees or escapes and travels secretly from place to place, and sometimes using disguises and aliases to conceal their identity,

fulfill.e: From Middle English fulfillen, from Old English fullfyllan (“to fill full”). By surface analysis, full- + fill.
fulfill.g: To satisfy, carry out, bring to completion (an obligation, a requirement, etc.).

full.e: From Middle English ful, from Old English full (“full”), from Proto-West Germanic *full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Germanic cognates include West Frisian fol, Low German vull, Dutch vol, German voll, Danish fuld, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish full.
full.g: Containing the maximum possible amount that can fit in the space available.

full.e: From Middle English fulle, fylle, fille, from Old English fyllu, fyllo (“fullness, fill, plenty”), from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄, *fulnō (“fullness, filling, overflow”), from Proto-Indo-European *plūno-, *plno- (“full”), from *pelh₁-, *pleh₁- (“to fill; full”).
full.g: Utmost measure or extent; highest state or degree; the state, position, or moment of fullness; fill.

full-grown.e: From Middle English *fulgrowen, fulgrowe, ful growe, equivalent to full + grown.

fuller.e: From Middle English fullere, from Old English fullere, from Latin fullō (“fuller”) + -ere; equivalent to full (“to densen cloth”) + -er.

fullness.e: From Middle English fulnesse, from Old English fulnes, fylnes, fyllnis (“completeness; abundance”), equivalent to full + -ness.

fully.e: From Middle English fully, fulliche, volliche, from Old English fullīċe (“fully”), equivalent to full + -ly.
fully.g: In a full manner; without lack or defect; completely, entirely.

fully.e: A reference to the phrase "the prisoner was fully committed for trial".
fully.g: To commit or send someone to trial.

function.e: From Middle French function, from Old French fonction, from Latin functiō (“performance, execution”), from functus, perfect participle of fungor (“to perform, execute, discharge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to enjoy”).
function.g: What something does or is used for.

fund.e: PIE word bʰudʰmḗn Borrowed from Latin fundus.
fund.g: A sum or source of money.

funeral.e: Borrowed from Middle French funerailles pl (“funeral rites”), from Medieval Latin fūnerālia (“funeral rites”), originally neuter plural of Late Latin fūnerālis (“having to do with a funeral”), from Latin fūnus (“funeral, death, corpse”), origin unknown, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- (“to die”).
funeral.g: A ceremony to honor and remember a deceased person, often distinguished from a memorial service by the presence of the body of the deceased.

fur.e: From Middle English furre, forre, from Anglo-Norman forre, fuerre (“case; sheath”), from Frankish *fōdar, from Proto-West Germanic *fōdr, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath”) (compare Old English fōdor (“sheaf”), Dutch voering (“lining”), German Futter (“lining”), Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐌳𐍂 (fōdr, “sheath”)).
fur.g: The hairy coat of various mammal species, especially when fine, soft and thick.

furbish.e: From Middle English furbisshen, from Old French forbir (stem furbiss-, “to clean, polish”), from Frankish *furbēn (“to clean, polish”).

furious.e: From Middle English furious, from Old French furieus, from Latin furiōsus.

furiously.e: From Middle English furiously; equivalent to furious + -ly.

furlong.e: From Middle English furlong, forlong (“unit of distance about one-eighth of a mile; quantity of land equal to one square furlong; racetrack for foot races; foot race”), from Old English furlang, furlung, from furh (“a furrow”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“to dig; to open.
furlong.g: A unit of distance equal to one-eighth of a mile (220 yards, or 201.168 metres), now mainly used in measuring distances in farmland and hors

furnace.e: From Middle English forneys, borrowed from Old French fornais, from Latin fornāx.
furnace.g: An industrial heating device, such as for smelting metal or firing ceramics.

furnish.e: From Middle English furnysshen, from Old French furniss-, stem of certain parts of furnir, fornir (Modern French fournir), from Germanic, from Frankish *frumjan (“to complete, execute”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną (“to further, promote”), from Proto-Indo-European *promo- (“front, forward”).
furnish.g: Material used to create an engineered product.

furniture.e: From Middle French fourniture (“a supply, or the act of furnishing”), from fournir (“to furnish”).
furniture.g: Large movable item(s), usually in a room, which enhance(s) the room's characteristics, functionally or decoratively.

furrow.e: From Middle English forow, furgh, from Old English furh, from Proto-West Germanic *furh, from Proto-Germanic *furhs (compare Saterland Frisian Fuurge, Dutch voor, German Furche, Swedish fåra, Norwegian Bokmål fure), from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“to dig”).
furrow.g: Any trench, channel, or groove; often found on wood or metal.

further.e: From Middle English further, forther, from Old English forþor, furþor (“further”, adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *furþer, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (a common preposition), equivalent to fore + -ther (a vestigial comparative ending still present in such words as other, either, whether, and, in altered form, in after).

furthermore.e: From Middle English furthermore, forthermore, forthermar (also as forther mo), equivalent to further + -more.
furthermore.g: In addition; besides; further; what's more (i.e. to denote additional information).

fury.e: From Middle English furie, from Old French furie, from Latin furia (“rage”).

futile.e: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.
futile.g: Incapable of producing results, useless; doomed not to be successful; not worth attempting.

futility.e: From Latin fūtilitās (“worthlessness, futility”). By surface analysis, futile + -ity.
futility.g: The quality of being futile or useless.

future.e: From Middle English future, futur, from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”).
future.g: The time ahead; those moments yet to be experienced.
